turn_text: Let's talk about the budget appropriations process because that is really important and the power of the purse is one of Congress's most important authorities under Article 1. So why is it so important to have a normal appropriations and budget process as opposed to just continuing resolutions which have funded the government for the last number of years?

Well, one, it is a waste of taxpayer money when you have the approach that you have. So let me give you an example. The largest employer in the district I represent is the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard in particular is the largest employer. Every time Congress comes up on a deadline, the Puget Sound Naval Shipyard actually has to plan for a potential government shutdown. When there is a continuing resolution, as you saw this past September, where Congress, in essence, kicks the can to December, what that means is when an entity, including Puget Sound Naval Shipyard, contracts for services, rather than contracting for a year worth of vet service, it contracts for whatever length of time that continuing resolution is. So think about it in your own life. When you buy the one-year plan or you buy the six-week plan, when do you pay a higher price and when do you pay a lower price? We pay a higher price because we're funding government six weeks, eight weeks at a time. Sometimes a few days at a time as Congress kicks the can. That is not efficient, and it makes it very difficult for the purposes of planning. Unfortunately, this has become commonplace. I would also add, and for those who are sort of constitutionalists, what you've seen is a whole bunch of power moved from the legislative branch to the executive branch, including the power of the purse. I mean, you have now federal agencies making spending decisions impacting my community and communities around the country. without as much input from members of Congress. So we made recommendations in that regard too, not to restore an old earmark process that had abuse and was not as transparent as it ought to be, but to set up a new system that we called community focused grant program. One that would enable congressionally directed spending in local communities, but in a way that was transparent, that would prevent abuse, and that would have, consistent with the views of the founders, members of Congress making decisions about spending specifically with regard to decisions impacting their own district rather than folks who are maybe well intentioned but are sitting in marble buildings 3,000 miles away from my district.

turn_text: That's great. So I have one final question for you, which is, what do you know now that you wish you knew during your transition into Congress.

It's a great question. I wish I had a good answer to it. I've learned a lot about both when this place works, why it works, and sometimes I've learned why it doesn't. You see very obvious instances of dysfunction And I think some of it is related to the ability to constructively engage members of Congress so that they are not destructively engaged. The Kilmer family has a new puppy. We, like many families, got a pandemic puppy. Australian Shepherd Penny is adorable. But I've discovered that if you don't constructively engage Penny, she'd choose the furniture. That kind of happens in Congress too. When people don't feel invested and engaged, they, to the furniture, right? They engage in things that contribute to incivility and contribute to dysfunction. That really shaped how, how, Our committee functioned. You know, Tom Graves, who served as our vice chair, and I made some conscious decisions early on in this process. And that was to truly have a bipartisan committee. Our committee ended up recommending things to encourage more bipartisan collaboration and more productivity. But we modeled those things ourselves. So let me give you some examples. You know, we, when a committee is established in Congress, they get it. They get a budget. And what generally happens is. the budget is split between the Democrats and the Republicans. Democrats use their part of the money to hire people with a Democratic background who put on blue jerseys, Republicans use their part to hire people with Republican backgrounds who put on red jerseys, and then they spend the rest of the time duking it out with one another. We consciously made a different decision. We said, let's have one nonpartisan staff, one budget, one office, no red jerseys or blue jerseys. Everybody's going to put on a fixed Congress jersey. And that was really constructive. You know, we hired our staff together. And some of them were people with Democratic backgrounds, some with Republican backgrounds. We held a bipartisan agenda setting retreat shortly after we were formed, and it really helped us establish a positive bipartisan approach to our work. from the outset. That was really valuable. We worked as partners. Vice Chair Graves and I worked as partners. Our committee members worked as partners. So we would spin off a Democrat and Republican to work on technology reforms or on staffing reforms or on civility reforms. And that actually encouraged bipartisan collaboration. We would meet regularly in private as a full committee. And what that meant is we were allowed to have some honest conversations and sometimes some really tough debates about how do you reform the budget and appropriations process? What do you do to solve some of these problems? But having those discussions in private, one, doesn't happen enough in Congress and two, can be really useful in terms of building trust between members. You know, we also experimented with some small but not insignificant things like mixed seating arrangements during our hearings. So rather than having Democrats sit on one side of the dais and Republicans sit on the other, we had Democrats and Republicans sit side by side. So why was that important? Well, what it meant was in the middle of a hearing when you heard someone testify and say something interesting, You logically leaned over to the person next to you and said, gosh, what do you think of that? That was kind of interesting. And it just so happened that the person sitting next to you was from the other party. And that really helped encourage bipartisan dialogue and civility. of that may sound like rocket science to you or to your listeners, but it's really unique in terms of how Congress functions or often doesn't function. And it means that both parties gave something up. As a member of the majority party, I gave up the right to just steamroll over the minority. But the minority gave something up too. And that is they gave up the ability to just sit on the sidelines and just vote no. You know, and they gave up the ability to chew on the furniture, right? They were invested in the outcome and engaged in the process. And I think that was a real lesson learned at the end of this process for me. And I hope is an instructive lesson for other committees to, if you want to be productive and have constructive engagement, there are some ways to do it.
